name: ZITLAS Zunka Bhakri Bowl
description: Dry, crumbly besan zunka served with jowar bhakri — a Maharashtrian staple combination reframed as a protein-and-fiber breakfast bowl.
ingredients: Mustard seeds, turmeric, green chilli — 4 g
instructions: Knead jowar flour with warm water and pat into a bhakri; cook on a hot tawa until browned on both sides.
Heat oil, temper mustard seeds, saute onion and green chilli until soft.
Sprinkle in besan gradually while stirring continuously to avoid lumps, along with turmeric and a little water, cooking until dry and crumbly (this is zunka, not a wet gravy).
Serve the zunka hot alongside the bhakri.
why_it_works: Zunka's dry, crumbly texture is genuinely different from a wet besan gravy like kadhi or pithla
Jowar bhakri is naturally gluten-free and fiber-rich
Everyday Maharashtrian farmer's meal, genuinely practical

name: ZITLAS Pithla Bhakri Bowl
description: A wet, gravy-like besan pithla served with bhakri — distinct from the dry zunka by its looser, saucier consistency.
ingredients: Garlic, cumin seeds, green chilli — 5 g
instructions: Knead jowar flour with warm water and pat into a bhakri; cook on a hot tawa.
Heat oil, temper cumin seeds, garlic and green chilli.
Whisk besan with water into a thin batter and pour in, stirring continuously until it thickens into a smooth, pourable gravy (looser than zunka).
Serve hot with the bhakri.
why_it_works: Deliberately looser, gravy-like consistency makes this a genuinely different eating experience from the dry zunka in this batch
Same core ingredients, different water ratio and technique
Traditional comfort food, quick to prepare

name: ZITLAS Tarri Poha
description: A Nagpur-style spicy poha topped with a thin, fiery tarri (gravy) — distinct from the standard kanda poha already in the database by the added spiced gravy layer.
ingredients: Nagpuri tarri masala (red chilli, garlic) — 5 g
instructions: Rinse poha and set aside.
For the tarri, heat oil, saute half the onion and all the tomato with the fiery Nagpuri masala, adding water to form a thin, spicy gravy; simmer 8-10 minutes.
Separately temper the remaining onion and peanuts in a little oil, then toss with the poha as usual.
Serve the poha topped with a generous ladle of hot tarri.
why_it_works: The tarri topping is a genuinely distinct Nagpur specialty not resembling the plain tempered poha already in the database
Vidarbha's famously fiery spice profile, different from Western Maharashtra's milder poha
Two-component dish rather than a single tempered preparation

name: ZITLAS Amboli
description: A thick, fermented rice-and-urad pancake from the Konkan coast — spongier and thicker than a dosa, with a distinct fermented tang.
instructions: Soak rice and urad dal separately for several hours, then grind together with a little cooked rice (this gives amboli its characteristic softness) into a thick batter.
Ferment overnight at room temperature.
Heat a tawa, pour a thick ladle of batter and spread only slightly — amboli stays thick, unlike a dosa.
Cover and cook until the top is set and full of small holes, then flip briefly.
Serve with coconut chutney.
Note: soak and overnight ferment folded into prep time above.
why_it_works: Thicker, spongier texture with a distinct fermented tang from Konkan coastal cooking, genuinely different from the thin, crisp dosas already in the database
Adding cooked rice to the batter is a specific regional technique that changes the final texture
Coastal Maharashtra rarely represented in fitness recipe collections

name: ZITLAS Ghavan
description: A thin, unfermented rice crepe from the Konkan region — distinct from amboli by being thin and quick, needing no fermentation wait.
instructions: Whisk rice flour with water into a thin, watery batter; rest 10 minutes.
Heat a tawa, pour a thin layer of batter and spread quickly like a dosa.
Cook until the edges lift, without needing to flip.
Serve warm, often with grated coconut and jaggery, or a savoury curry.
why_it_works: No fermentation wait, unlike amboli, making this a genuinely faster Konkan breakfast option
Thin, delicate texture distinct from the thick amboli or a crisp dosa
Traditionally served both sweet and savoury depending on the accompaniment

name: ZITLAS Dhirde
description: A savoury multi-flour crepe combining rice flour and besan — a distinct batter composition from either amboli or ghavan in this batch.
instructions: Whisk rice flour and besan with water into a thin batter; mix in onion, cumin seeds and green chilli.
Heat a tawa, pour a thin layer of batter and spread quickly.
Cook until golden on both sides with a little oil.
Serve with chutney.
why_it_works: Combining rice flour and besan gives dhirde more protein than the plain rice-based ghavan, a genuinely different composition
Savoury, onion-forward flavour distinct from the plain or coconut-topped ghavan
Quick, one-pan preparation

name: ZITLAS Patal Bhaji Bhakri Bowl
description: A thin, watery mixed-vegetable curry served with bhakri — a lighter, soupier vegetable preparation than a standard sabzi.
instructions: Knead jowar flour with warm water and pat into a bhakri; cook on a hot tawa.
Heat oil, saute the vegetables briefly, then add goda masala and a generous amount of water to keep it thin and soupy.
Simmer 10-12 minutes.
Serve the thin curry hot with the bhakri, tearing pieces of bhakri into the bowl if liked.
why_it_works: Deliberately thin, brothy consistency is a distinct style of Maharashtrian vegetable cooking from a standard dry or semi-dry sabzi
Goda masala gives a distinctly Maharashtrian sweet-spicy flavour profile
Comforting, easy-to-digest breakfast

name: ZITLAS Kothimbir Vadi Bowl
description: Steamed besan-and-coriander vadi, sliced and lightly pan-tempered — a snack traditionally fried, made lighter here as a breakfast bowl.
ingredients: Sesame seeds, turmeric, green chilli — 4 g
instructions: Whisk besan with chopped coriander, turmeric, green chilli and water into a thick batter.
Pour into a greased tin and steam in a pressure cooker (without the whistle) for 12-15 minutes until firm.
Cool slightly, cut into diamond-shaped pieces.
Heat a little oil in a tawa, temper sesame seeds, and lightly pan-toast the vadi pieces on both sides.
Serve warm.
why_it_works: Steaming first and pan-toasting after gives a genuinely lighter result than the traditional deep-fried vadi
Coriander-forward flavour distinct from any other besan preparation in the database
Popular Maharashtrian snack reframed as a substantial breakfast

name: ZITLAS Alu Vadi (Patra) Steamed Rolls
description: Colocasia (arbi) leaves spread with a spiced besan paste, rolled and steamed, then sliced — a distinct leaf-wrapped steamed format not used anywhere else in the database.
instructions: Make a thick, spiced besan paste with tamarind, jaggery, turmeric and chilli powder.
Spread the paste evenly over each colocasia leaf, stack them, and roll tightly into a log.
Steam the rolled log in a pressure cooker (without the whistle) for 20-25 minutes.
Cool slightly, slice into rounds, and pan-toast lightly in oil before serving.
why_it_works: Using a leaf as the wrapping vessel is genuinely unlike any roll, roti or wrap elsewhere in the database
Tamarind-jaggery balance gives a distinct sweet-tangy Maharashtrian flavour
Traditional technique requiring a specific vegetable (colocasia leaves) not used in any other recipe

name: ZITLAS Rava Sheera Protein Bowl
description: A portion-controlled semolina sheera made with less ghee than traditional and a spoon of milk powder for extra protein — a sweet Maharashtrian breakfast staple made more fitness-conscious.
instructions: Heat ghee in a kadai, roast the rava on low heat for 3-4 minutes until aromatic.
Add milk gradually, stirring continuously to avoid lumps.
Once thickened, stir in milk powder and jaggery, cooking 2-3 more minutes.
Serve warm.
why_it_works: Milk powder addition raises the protein meaningfully above a traditional sheera
Deliberately less ghee than the usual festive version
Familiar comfort food made into a genuine breakfast rather than an occasional dessert

name: ZITLAS Dahi Ambil
description: A fermented bajra porridge mixed with curd — a traditional Maharashtrian probiotic breakfast drink-bowl, distinct from any other millet or curd preparation in the database.
ingredients: Roasted cumin powder, black salt — 2 g
instructions: Whisk bajra flour with water and let it ferment at room temperature for at least 8-12 hours (or overnight).
Cook the fermented mixture gently for 8-10 minutes until it thickens slightly, then cool.
Mix in curd, roasted cumin powder and black salt.
Serve chilled or at room temperature.
Note: fermentation time folded into prep above.
why_it_works: Fermented bajra base gives this a genuinely different, tangier profile from the plain or malt versions of millet drinks already in the database
Traditional probiotic breakfast, distinct from any curd-rice or curd-oats preparation
Cooling, good for hot Maharashtrian summers

name: ZITLAS Patodi
description: Steamed besan squares in a Maharashtrian spice blend, cut thicker than khaman or dhokla and tempered with sesame — a distinct regional variation on steamed besan.
instructions: Whisk besan with curd, water and turmeric into a thick batter.
Pour into a greased tin and steam in a pressure cooker (without the whistle) for 12-15 minutes.
Cool slightly and cut into thick squares (patodi is cut thicker than khaman or dhokla).
Temper sesame seeds in oil and pour over the top before serving.
why_it_works: Thicker cut and sesame tempering give patodi a distinctly different texture and flavour from the fluffy Khaman or grainy Rava Dhokla already in the database
Curd in the batter raises the protein
Maharashtrian regional variation on a widely-used besan technique

name: ZITLAS Solkadhi and Roasted Chana Combo
description: A cooling kokum-and-coconut-milk drink from the Konkan coast, paired with a side of roasted chana for protein — a distinct drink-plus-snack breakfast combination.
instructions: Soak kokum in a little warm water to extract its colour and tang.
Whisk the kokum water into coconut milk along with garlic, cumin and green chilli, thinning with plain water to a drinkable consistency.
Serve chilled in a glass, alongside a small bowl of roasted chana for protein.
why_it_works: Kokum is a genuinely distinct souring agent from tamarind or lemon used elsewhere in the database, specific to Konkan cooking
Solkadhi alone is very light on protein, so pairing it with roasted chana makes this a more complete breakfast
Very cooling, ideal for hot coastal mornings

name: ZITLAS Savoury Steamed Rice Dumplings with Moong Filling
description: A modak-inspired steamed rice-flour dumpling filled with spiced moong dal instead of the traditional sweet coconut-jaggery filling — a savoury adaptation of the iconic Maharashtrian shape.
ingredients: Moong dal, cooked and mashed — 60 g
instructions: Knead rice flour with boiling water into a smooth, pliable dough (the same technique used for sweet modak).
Mix cooked mashed moong dal with cumin seeds and green chilli for the filling.
Shape small discs of dough, pleat the edges, fill with the moong mixture, and gather into the traditional modak shape.
Steam in a pressure cooker (without the whistle) for 12-15 minutes.
Serve warm with a little ghee.
why_it_works: Explicitly a savoury reinterpretation of a beloved festive sweet shape, giving it a genuine everyday protein-forward purpose
Steamed, no added fat beyond a light ghee drizzle
Distinct construction technique (pleating) not used in any other recipe in the database

name: ZITLAS Farsan-Free Sprouts Misal Bowl
description: A lighter version of misal made from sprouted matki without the usual pav or fried farsan topping — a genuinely different composition from the Misal Pav Bowl already in the database.
instructions: Heat oil, saute onion until golden, add tomato and cook soft.
Add boiled matki and goda masala with a little water; simmer 8-10 minutes into a moderately thick gravy.
Serve hot in a bowl with a squeeze of lemon — no pav, no farsan, keeping this lighter and more protein-dense per calorie.
why_it_works: Removing the pav and fried farsan meaningfully changes both the calorie and carbohydrate profile from the Misal Pav Bowl already in the database
Higher protein-to-calorie ratio for a weight-loss-focused user
Same base legume, genuinely different composition and purpose

name: ZITLAS Vangyache Bharit Toast
description: Smoky, open-flame-roasted eggplant mash spread on toast — a distinct vegetable and roasting technique not used anywhere else in the database.
instructions: Roast the whole eggplant directly over an open gas flame, turning occasionally, until the skin is charred and the inside is soft, about 10-12 minutes.
Peel off the charred skin and mash the smoky flesh.
Mix in onion, green chilli, coriander and a little oil.
Toast the bread and spread the bharit generously over it.
why_it_works: Open-flame roasting gives a genuinely smoky flavour that no other vegetable preparation in the database has
Very low calorie, high fiber vegetable base
Traditional Maharashtrian bharit technique applied to a toast format instead of the usual bhakri pairing

name: ZITLAS Maharashtrian Methi Bhakri
description: A millet flatbread with fresh fenugreek leaves kneaded directly into the dough — distinct from the wheat-based methi theplas and parathas already in the database by using jowar or bajra flour instead.
instructions: Knead jowar flour with chopped methi leaves, green chilli and warm water into a soft dough.
Pat out by hand into a thick round (bhakri is patted, not rolled with a pin).
Cook on a hot tawa until browned on both sides, brushing with a little oil.
Serve hot with curd or pickle.
why_it_works: Millet-flour base is a genuinely different grain from the wheat used in the existing methi thepla or paratha, changing both texture and glycemic profile
Hand-patted bhakri technique produces a denser bread than a rolled roti
Traditional Maharashtrian everyday food

name: ZITLAS Nagpuri Saoji-Style Egg Curry Bowl
description: Boiled eggs simmered in a fiery Vidarbha-style saoji spice paste, known for its distinctive dry-roasted whole spice blend — a genuinely different regional egg curry from the Bengali, Chettinad or standard North Indian versions already in the database.
ingredients: Dry-roasted whole spices (coriander, cumin, dried red chilli) — 6 g
instructions: Dry-roast the whole spices in a pan until fragrant, then grind to a coarse powder.
Heat oil, fry sliced onion until deep golden, then blend with garlic, ginger and the roasted spice powder into a thick paste.
Return the paste to the kadai, add water to form a gravy, and simmer 8-10 minutes.
Halve the boiled eggs and simmer in the gravy for 3-4 minutes.
Serve hot.
why_it_works: Saoji's dry-roasted whole-spice technique is a genuinely distinct regional method from every other egg curry already in the database
Famously one of Vidarbha's spiciest culinary traditions, offering real flavour variety
Deep-fried onion paste base gives a distinctly different gravy texture

name: ZITLAS Baked Kombdi Vade Chicken Bowl
description: A Kolhapur-style spiced chicken curry served with baked (not deep-fried) puri — a lighter adaptation of the iconic Kolhapuri breakfast combination.
instructions: Knead atta into a firm dough, roll small discs, and bake at 200°C for 10-12 minutes until puffed and lightly golden (a baked stand-in for the traditional fried vade).
Heat oil, fry onion until golden, add ginger-garlic paste and Kolhapuri masala, then the chicken.
Add water and simmer 12-15 minutes until the chicken is cooked through.
Serve the curry hot with the baked vade.
why_it_works: Baking the puri instead of deep-frying is a genuine practical adaptation that meaningfully cuts the fat of this iconic Kolhapur breakfast
Kolhapuri masala's distinctive fiery red-chilli blend is a genuinely different spice profile from any other chicken curry already in the database
Complete, filling regional breakfast

name: ZITLAS Aamras Protein Bowl
description: Fresh mango pulp mixed with Greek yogurt — a Maharashtrian summer specialty (aamras) given a protein boost, distinct from the plain Mango Lassi Protein Bowl by texture and lack of dilution.
instructions: Pulp the mango by hand or with a fork (aamras is traditionally not blended smooth like a lassi).
Fold in Greek yogurt and cardamom powder.
Serve at room temperature or lightly chilled, with a bhakri or puri if available.
why_it_works: Deliberately less-blended texture keeps this closer to traditional aamras than the smooth lassi bowl already in the database
Maharashtrian summer festival food made into an everyday protein-forward breakfast
Very simple, minimal ingredients

name: ZITLAS Varan Bhaat Bowl
description: Simple, comforting toor dal cooked plain and served over rice with a little ghee — Maharashtra's everyday lunch staple, genuinely different from any spiced dal preparation elsewhere in the database.
instructions: Pressure cook toor dal with turmeric and water for 3-4 whistles until very soft.
Lightly mash the dal and temper with cumin seeds in ghee.
Serve the plain varan over warm rice with an extra drizzle of ghee.
why_it_works: Deliberately unspiced and simple, a genuinely different style from every masala-heavy dal dish in the database
The most everyday, foundational Maharashtrian lunch, prepared almost daily in most homes
Easy to digest, gentle on the stomach

name: ZITLAS Amti Bhaat Bowl
description: A tangy, spiced Kolhapuri-style dal with goda masala and kokum, served over rice — distinctly more complex and sour than the plain Varan Bhaat in this batch.
instructions: Pressure cook toor dal until soft.
Heat oil, temper with goda masala, then add the cooked dal, kokum and a little jaggery, along with water to loosen.
Simmer 8-10 minutes to let the flavours combine.
Serve hot over rice.
why_it_works: Goda masala and kokum give amti a distinctly sweet-sour-spicy profile, genuinely different from the plain Varan or any North Indian dal in the database
Kolhapuri specialty, more complex in flavour than everyday varan
Same base legume, deliberately different technique and seasoning

name: ZITLAS Bharli Vangi with Bhakri
description: Baby eggplants stuffed with a spiced peanut-coconut masala and simmered, served with bhakri — a distinct stuffed-vegetable curry technique not used anywhere else in the database.
instructions: Knead jowar flour into a bhakri and cook on a tawa.
Slit the baby brinjals lengthwise without cutting through, keeping the stem intact.
Mix ground peanuts, grated coconut and goda masala into a thick stuffing paste, and fill each brinjal.
Heat oil in a kadai, place the stuffed brinjals in, add a little water, cover and simmer 15-18 minutes until tender.
Serve hot with the bhakri.
why_it_works: The peanut-coconut stuffing technique is genuinely distinct from any other vegetable preparation in the database
Whole stuffed baby eggplants rather than chopped vegetable is a different cooking approach entirely
Iconic Maharashtrian festive dish reframed as an everyday lunch

name: ZITLAS Kolhapuri Pandhra Rassa Chicken Bowl
description: A mild, white coconut-based Kolhapuri chicken curry — one half of the famous Kolhapuri rassa pair, distinctly milder than its red counterpart.
ingredients: Whole spices (no red chilli), poppy seeds — 5 g
instructions: Grind grated coconut with poppy seeds and a little water into a smooth white paste.
Heat oil, saute onion until soft (without browning too much, to keep the gravy pale), add whole spices.
Add the chicken and cook 5 minutes, then stir in the coconut paste and water; simmer 15-18 minutes until the chicken is tender.
Serve hot, deliberately mild and creamy rather than spicy.
why_it_works: Pandhra rassa's defining feature is its mildness and pale colour, achieved by avoiding red chilli and browning — a genuinely distinct technique from every other chicken curry in the database
Traditionally served alongside the spicy tambda rassa as a cooling contrast
Coconut-poppy seed base gives real textural richness without excess oil

name: ZITLAS Kolhapuri Tambda Rassa Chicken Bowl
description: A fiery red Kolhapuri chicken curry, the spicier counterpart to the pandhra rassa in this batch — deep red from a specific dried-chilli paste, genuinely distinct in both colour and heat.
ingredients: Dried Kolhapuri red chillies, ground — 8 g
instructions: Deep-fry or dry-roast the sliced onion until dark golden, then blend with dried Kolhapuri chillies, garlic, ginger and a little coconut into a thick, deep red paste.
Heat oil, add the paste and cook until the oil separates.
Add the chicken and water, and simmer 18-20 minutes until tender and the gravy is deep red and thick.
Serve hot — this is deliberately the spicier, more intense curry of the Kolhapuri pair.
why_it_works: The specific dried-chilli paste and deep-fried onion base are what give tambda rassa its famous heat and colour, genuinely different from the mild pandhra rassa in this batch
One of India's most famous fiery curries, offering real spice-level variety for users who want it
The two rassa recipes are traditionally served together, so both are included as a legitimate pair

name: ZITLAS Malvani Fish Curry Rice Bowl
description: A spicy, coconut-and-kokum-based Malvani fish curry from the Konkan coast — distinct from the milder Bengali, Kerala or Assamese fish curries already in the database.
instructions: Grind grated coconut with Malvani masala and garlic into a thick red paste.
Heat oil, add the paste and cook until fragrant.
Add water and kokum, bring to a simmer, then gently add the fish and cook 6-8 minutes until just cooked through.
Serve over warm rice.
why_it_works: Malvani masala's specific spice blend and kokum's tang give this a genuinely distinct flavour profile from every other fish curry in the database
Konkan coastal cooking style, spicier and more coconut-forward than the Kerala or Bengali versions already represented
Kokum instead of tamarind or lemon as the souring agent is a regionally specific choice

name: ZITLAS Malvani Prawn Sukka
description: A dry, intensely spiced prawn preparation from the Konkan coast — distinct from the wet Prawn Curry Rice Bowl and Prawn Biryani already in the database by its dry, coconut-coated texture.
instructions: Heat oil, saute onion until golden.
Add Malvani masala and grated coconut, roasting for 2-3 minutes until fragrant.
Add the prawns and cook on medium-high heat for 5-6 minutes, tossing continuously, until the prawns are cooked and the mixture is dry, not saucy.
Serve hot as a dry side with rice or bhakri.
why_it_works: Sukka's dry, coconut-coated technique is genuinely different from the wet-gravy prawn preparations already in the database
Prawns cook very fast, so this dry method concentrates flavour quickly without a long simmer
Distinct texture — clingy and roasted, not saucy

name: ZITLAS Kombdi Sukka
description: Dry, deeply roasted spiced chicken with coconut — a distinct dry-preparation technique from the wet Kolhapuri rassa curries already in this batch.
instructions: Heat oil, saute onion until deep golden.
Add masala and grated coconut, roasting until fragrant.
Add the chicken and a small splash of water, cover and cook 18-20 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the chicken is tender and the mixture has dried down and roasted.
Serve as a dry side dish.
why_it_works: Dry sukka technique is genuinely different from the wet gravy of the pandhra and tambda rassa already in this batch, giving users a textural choice for the same protein
Roasted coconut coating concentrates flavour without a thin gravy
Traditional accompaniment to bhakri

name: ZITLAS Matki Chi Usal Lunchbox Bowl
description: A dry-cooked sprouted matki usal specifically thickened and reduced so it travels well in a lunchbox for several hours — distinct from the breakfast-format Matki Usal Bowl by its consistency and purpose.
instructions: Heat oil, saute onion until golden, add goda masala.
Add boiled matki with only a small splash of water, and cook down until thick and dry rather than saucy, about 10-12 minutes — this dryness is what makes it travel well.
Pack while warm into a lunchbox.
Eat within a few hours, at room temperature or reheated.
why_it_works: Deliberately dry-cooked (unlike a home-eaten wet usal) so it doesn't leak or spoil as fast in a packed lunchbox
Designed specifically around the office/college lunchbox constraint rather than immediate home eating
High protein and fiber for a sustained afternoon

name: ZITLAS Val (Lilva Beans) Usal Bowl
description: A tempered curry made from val (field beans) — introducing a legume not used anywhere else in the database, prepared usal-style.
instructions: Heat oil, saute onion and garlic until golden, add goda masala.
Add boiled val beans with a little water and simmer 8-10 minutes.
Serve hot with rice or bhakri.
why_it_works: Val (field beans) is a genuinely new legume for the database, with a distinct earthy flavour from moong, chana or matki
Winter-season Maharashtrian legume, adding real seasonal and nutritional variety
Same reliable usal technique applied to a new pulse

name: ZITLAS Masoor Usal Bowl
description: A tempered masoor dal usal — a distinct legume choice from the moong, matki, chana, or val usals already used in the database.
ingredients: Masoor dal, boiled (whole, not split) — 130 g
instructions: Heat oil, saute onion until golden, add goda masala.
Add boiled whole masoor and a little water, simmering 6-8 minutes.
Serve hot with rice or bhakri.
why_it_works: Whole masoor (not split red lentil) is a distinct legume choice from any usal already in the database
Quick-cooking compared to matki or val, good for a faster lunch
Same reliable usal technique, different pulse each time

name: ZITLAS Alu Panchamrut Vegetable Bowl
description: A five-vegetable Maharashtrian curry combining brinjal, potato, beans and other seasonal vegetables in a single spiced gravy — a distinct multi-vegetable combination dish.
instructions: Heat oil, temper with goda masala.
Add all the vegetables together and saute 3-4 minutes.
Add a little water and simmer 15-18 minutes until all vegetables are tender.
Stir in crushed peanuts for texture and protein.
Serve hot with bhakri or rice.
why_it_works: Combining five distinct vegetables in one pot is a genuinely different composition from any single-vegetable curry in the database
Peanuts stirred in at the end add protein and crunch not usually found in a mixed-vegetable sabzi
Traditional Maharashtrian technique of building flavour across multiple vegetables at once

name: ZITLAS Zunka Bhakri Family Thali
description: A larger, thali-format version of zunka bhakri with sides of curd, salad and pickle — a shared family meal format distinct from the individual breakfast bowl already in the database.
instructions: Make three bhakris from the jowar flour, cooking each on a hot tawa.
Prepare a larger batch of zunka as in the breakfast version, scaled up for three servings.
Plate as a thali with the bhakris, zunka, and simple sides like sliced onion or curd.
Serve family-style for sharing.
why_it_works: Scaled for sharing across a family rather than a single portion, a genuinely different meal-planning purpose from the individual breakfast bowl
Thali format with sides changes the eating experience from a simple bowl
Same core recipe, different serving context and scale

name: ZITLAS Soya Chi Bhaji with Bhakri
description: Soya chunks cooked in a Maharashtrian-style onion-tomato gravy with goda masala, served with bhakri — a distinct regional treatment of soya from the keema, frankie or biryani preparations already in the database.
instructions: Knead jowar flour into a bhakri and cook on a tawa.
Heat oil, saute onion and tomato until soft, add goda masala.
Add the rehydrated soya chunks and a little water; simmer 8-10 minutes.
Serve hot with the bhakri.
why_it_works: Goda masala's specific sweet-spicy blend gives this soya preparation a genuinely different flavour direction from the keema, frankie or biryani soya recipes already in the database
Bhakri pairing (not roti or rice) is a distinctly Maharashtrian meal structure
High protein, budget-friendly

name: ZITLAS Maharashtrian Kadhi Bhaat Bowl
description: A besan-and-curd kadhi with a distinctly Maharashtrian sweet-and-mild spice profile, served over rice — different from the tangier Gujarati-style Besan Kadhi Bowl already in the database.
ingredients: Jaggery, mustard seeds, curry leaves — 5 g
instructions: Whisk besan into curd and water until smooth.
Heat oil, temper mustard seeds and curry leaves.
Pour in the besan-curd mixture, add a small piece of jaggery, and simmer gently, stirring often, for 10-12 minutes until thickened.
Serve over warm rice.
why_it_works: A touch of jaggery gives Maharashtrian kadhi a distinctly milder, slightly sweet profile compared to the tangier Gujarati kadhi already in the database
Curd base provides real protein
Comforting, easy-to-digest lunch

name: ZITLAS Vangi Bhaat
description: A one-pot eggplant-and-rice dish flavoured with goda masala — a distinct rice preparation from any pulao or biryani already in the database.
instructions: Heat oil, temper whole spices, add brinjal and peanuts, and saute 3-4 minutes.
Add rice and goda masala, mixing well.
Add water in the standard ratio and pressure cook for 2 whistles.
Fluff with a fork and serve hot.
why_it_works: Goda masala's specific sweet-spicy Maharashtrian blend distinguishes this from any other spiced rice dish in the database
Brinjal cooked directly into the rice, not as a separate side
One-pot, mostly hands-off preparation

name: ZITLAS Masale Bhaat
description: A spiced mixed-vegetable rice using goda masala and a wider vegetable mix than Vangi Bhaat, without eggplant as the dominant flavour — a distinct one-pot rice preparation from this batch's other rice dishes.
instructions: Heat oil, temper whole spices, add mixed vegetables and saute 3-4 minutes.
Add rice and goda masala, mixing well.
Add water in the standard ratio and pressure cook for 2 whistles.
Fluff with a fork and serve hot.
why_it_works: Uses a broader vegetable mix rather than being built around one dominant vegetable like the Vangi Bhaat in this batch
Same goda masala base but a genuinely different vegetable composition and flavour balance
Family-friendly, less intensely flavoured than vangi bhaat

name: ZITLAS Portion-Controlled Puran Poli with Protein Kadhi
description: A single small puran poli (sweet stuffed flatbread) paired specifically with a protein-rich kadhi side to balance the meal — a portion-controlled way to enjoy a traditionally rich festive sweet.
ingredients: Chana dal, cooked and mashed — 50 g
instructions: Cook mashed chana dal with jaggery into a thick, dry filling (puran).
Roll a small ball of atta dough thin, place a portion of puran in the centre, seal and roll out gently into a thin flatbread.
Cook on a hot tawa until lightly browned on both sides.
Separately whisk curd with besan and water, and simmer into a light kadhi.
Serve one small puran poli alongside a generous bowl of kadhi to balance the meal with protein.
why_it_works: Deliberately single, small-portion puran poli paired with a protein-forward kadhi, rather than multiple polis eaten alone, balances the traditionally rich sweet with real protein
Chana dal filling itself contributes some protein, unlike a purely sugar-based sweet
Festive dish made into a considered, portion-aware everyday meal

name: ZITLAS Konkan Fish Thali Bowl
description: A multi-component Konkan meal combining rice, a small fish curry portion, and a side of solkadhi — a distinct thali format bringing together several Konkan elements in one balanced bowl.
instructions: Cook a small portion of fish curry using coconut milk, kokum and Malvani masala, simmering the fish gently for 6-8 minutes.
Separately mix a little coconut milk with kokum water to make a small side of solkadhi.
Serve the fish curry over rice with the solkadhi alongside as a palate-cleansing drink.
why_it_works: Combining a curry, rice and a drink side into one considered thali is a genuinely different meal structure from a single fish-curry-and-rice bowl
Solkadhi traditionally aids digestion after a coconut-heavy meal, a purposeful pairing rather than a random addition
Represents a complete, authentic Konkan meal structure rather than one isolated dish

name: ZITLAS Chicken Kolhapuri Lunchbox Wrap
description: Kolhapuri-spiced shredded chicken wrapped in a roti, engineered specifically to hold together and travel for an office lunchbox — distinct from eating the same curry as a bowl at home.
ingredients: Chicken, lean, shredded after cooking — 100 g
instructions: Cook the chicken in oil with Kolhapuri masala until fully done, then shred it and cook down any liquid until the mixture is dry rather than saucy (this is what makes it travel well).
Roll out and roast the atta into a roti.
Spread the dry, spiced shredded chicken onto the roti with sliced onion, and roll tightly.
Wrap in foil — it holds together for several hours without leaking.
why_it_works: Deliberately dry-cooked and shredded (unlike the saucy Kolhapuri rassa curries in this batch) specifically so it works as a portable wrap
Kolhapuri spice intensity carries well even without a wet gravy
Designed around the actual constraint of an office lunchbox rather than home eating

name: ZITLAS Kolhapuri Mutton Rassa Bowl
description: A rich, spiced Kolhapuri mutton curry — introducing mutton in a genuine Kolhapuri preparation, distinct from the plainer Lean Mutton Curry Rice Bowl already in the database.
ingredients: Dried Kolhapuri red chillies, ground — 8 g
instructions: Fry sliced onion until deep golden, then blend with dried Kolhapuri chillies, garlic, ginger and coconut into a thick paste.
Heat oil, add the paste and cook until the oil separates.
Add the mutton and enough water to cover, then pressure cook for 15-18 minutes until tender.
Serve hot, deliberately spicy and deep red.
why_it_works: Kolhapuri masala's specific dried-chilli paste gives this a genuinely distinct regional identity from the simpler home-style mutton curry already in the database
Pressure cooking keeps mutton's usually long cooking time practical
One of Maharashtra's most iconic non-vegetarian dishes

name: ZITLAS Malvani Chicken Curry Bowl
description: A coconut-forward Konkan chicken curry, distinct from the drier Kombdi Sukka in this batch and the Kolhapuri rassa curries by its specific coastal spice blend.
instructions: Grind grated coconut with Malvani masala into a thick paste.
Heat oil, saute onion until golden, add the coconut paste and cook until fragrant.
Add the chicken and water, and simmer 18-20 minutes until tender.
Serve hot with rice or bhakri.
why_it_works: Malvani masala's coastal spice blend, heavier on coconut, is genuinely distinct from the deep-fried-onion-based Kolhapuri curries in this batch
Wet, saucy format distinct from the dry Kombdi Sukka
Konkan coastal identity, different from the inland Kolhapur style

name: ZITLAS Baked Bombil (Bombay Duck) Bowl
description: Bombil, the iconic Mumbai fish, coated in a light spiced batter and baked instead of the traditional deep-fry — introducing a distinct fish species not used anywhere else in the database.
ingredients: Turmeric, red chilli powder, semolina — 6 g
instructions: Marinate the bombil fillets with turmeric and red chilli powder.
Coat lightly in a mix of rice flour and semolina.
Arrange on a lightly oiled tray and bake at 200°C for 12-15 minutes, turning once, until crisp and cooked through.
Serve hot with a wedge of lemon.
why_it_works: Bombil (Bombay duck) is a genuinely distinct, delicate fish species iconic to Mumbai, not used anywhere else in the database
Baking instead of deep-frying keeps this meaningfully lighter than the traditional street-food preparation
Rice flour and semolina coating gives a crisp texture without the usual oil load

name: ZITLAS Surmai (Kingfish) Curry Rice Bowl
description: A Konkan-style curry using surmai (kingfish), a firmer, meatier fish than the lean fillets used elsewhere in the database — a distinct fish species and texture.
instructions: Heat oil, add Malvani masala and cook briefly.
Add coconut milk and a little water, bring to a simmer.
Add the surmai steak and cook gently for 8-10 minutes, turning once, until just cooked through (kingfish holds together better than delicate fillets).
Serve over warm rice.
why_it_works: Surmai's firm, meaty texture is genuinely different from the flakier lean fish used in every other fish curry in the database
A prized, popular Konkan fish offering real variety for non-vegetarian users
Holds its shape well through cooking, a distinct textural experience

name: ZITLAS Kolhapuri-Style Egg Curry Bowl
description: Boiled eggs simmered in a Kolhapuri masala gravy — distinct from the Nagpuri saoji, Bengali, Chettinad or standard egg curries already in the database by its specific dried-chilli paste base.
ingredients: Dried Kolhapuri red chillies, ground — 6 g
instructions: Fry sliced onion until golden, blend with dried Kolhapuri chillies, garlic and coconut into a paste.
Heat oil, cook the paste until the oil separates.
Add water to form a gravy and simmer 8-10 minutes.
Halve the boiled eggs and simmer in the gravy for 3-4 minutes.
Serve hot.
why_it_works: Kolhapuri masala's specific dried-chilli base gives this a genuinely different flavour identity from the Nagpuri saoji or Bengali panch-phoron egg curries already in the database
Same reliable curry technique used for chicken and mutton in this batch, applied to eggs for a budget-friendly protein option
Deep red, spicy Kolhapuri character

name: ZITLAS Soya Kolhapuri Bowl
description: Soya chunks cooked in a Kolhapuri-style spiced gravy — a vegetarian option using the same distinctive Kolhapuri paste as the meat and egg curries in this batch.
ingredients: Dried Kolhapuri red chillies, ground — 6 g
instructions: Fry sliced onion until golden, blend with dried Kolhapuri chillies, garlic and coconut into a paste.
Heat oil, cook the paste until fragrant.
Add the rehydrated soya chunks and water; simmer 10-12 minutes.
Serve hot with rice or bhakri.
why_it_works: Gives vegetarian and vegan users access to the same distinctive Kolhapuri flavour profile as the meat and egg versions in this batch
High protein, budget-friendly alternative to the meat curries
Same fiery regional character, different protein base

name: ZITLAS Paneer Kolhapuri Bowl
description: Paneer cubes simmered in Kolhapuri masala — a dairy-protein option within the same Kolhapuri flavour family as the soya, egg, chicken and mutton versions in this batch.
ingredients: Dried Kolhapuri red chillies, ground — 6 g
instructions: Fry sliced onion until golden, blend with dried Kolhapuri chillies, garlic and coconut into a paste.
Heat oil, cook the paste until fragrant.
Add water to form a gravy, then gently add the paneer cubes and simmer 5-6 minutes (avoid overcooking so the paneer stays soft).
Serve hot with rice or bhakri.
why_it_works: Completes the set of five distinct proteins (mutton, chicken, egg, soya, paneer) sharing the same Kolhapuri flavour base in this batch, letting users choose by preference or budget
Paneer's mild flavour absorbs the fiery masala well
Familiar protein in a genuinely regional preparation

name: ZITLAS Tofu Malvani Bowl
description: Tofu simmered in a coconut-based Malvani gravy — a vegan protein option using the Konkan coastal flavour profile rather than the inland Kolhapuri base used elsewhere in this batch.
instructions: Grind grated coconut with Malvani masala into a paste.
Heat oil, saute onion, add the coconut paste and cook until fragrant.
Add water to form a gravy, then gently add the tofu cubes and simmer 6-8 minutes.
Serve hot with rice.
why_it_works: Uses the Malvani (coastal) flavour profile rather than the Kolhapuri (inland) base used for the other proteins in this batch, giving genuine regional variety within Maharashtra itself
Fully vegan, high protein
Coconut-forward gravy pairs well with tofu's mild flavour

name: ZITLAS Chawli Usal Dinner Bowl
description: A tempered curry made from cooked cowpea (chawli), prepared usal-style — a warm, cooked dinner preparation distinct from the raw salad and cooked-roll uses of the same legume already in the database.
instructions: Heat oil, saute onion until golden, add goda masala.
Add boiled chawli with a little water and simmer 8-10 minutes.
Serve hot with bhakri or rice.
why_it_works: Usal preparation (tempered, moderately dry) gives chawli a third genuinely distinct role in the database, alongside its raw salad and gravy-roll uses
Goda masala ties this into the same Maharashtrian usal family as the matki, val and masoor versions
Warm, simple dinner preparation

name: ZITLAS Bhakri with Pithla Light Dinner
description: A lighter, dinner-portioned pithla and bhakri combination specifically kept smaller and less oily than the breakfast version — framed around an early, light evening meal.
instructions: Knead jowar flour into a smaller bhakri and cook on a tawa.
Heat oil, temper cumin seeds and garlic.
Whisk besan with water into a thin batter and pour in, stirring until it thickens into a smooth gravy.
Serve a modest portion hot with the bhakri — deliberately lighter than a full breakfast serving.
why_it_works: Deliberately smaller portions and less oil than the breakfast Pithla Bhakri Bowl already in the database, appropriate for a lighter evening meal
Same core dish, different portioning philosophy for a different time of day
Easy to digest before sleep

name: ZITLAS Malvani Prawns Curry Bowl
description: A wet, coconut-based Malvani prawn curry — the saucy counterpart to the dry Malvani Prawn Sukka in this batch's lunch section, giving users a textural choice for the same protein.
instructions: Grind grated coconut with Malvani masala into a paste.
Heat oil, saute onion, add the coconut paste and cook until fragrant.
Add water to form a gravy, then add the prawns and simmer just 4-5 minutes until pink and cooked through.
Serve over rice.
why_it_works: Wet, saucy format is a deliberate contrast to the dry Malvani Prawn Sukka in this batch's lunch section, giving genuine textural choice for the same protein and region
Prawns cook fast, keeping this a realistically quick dinner despite the gravy
Classic Konkan coastal preparation

name: ZITLAS Vidarbha-Style Chicken Rassa Bowl
description: A Vidarbha-region chicken curry with its own distinct spice character, separate from the Kolhapuri pandhra and tambda rassa already in this batch — offering a third regional Maharashtrian chicken curry style.
ingredients: Dry-roasted whole spices (coriander, sesame, dried chilli) — 6 g
instructions: Dry-roast whole spices including sesame seeds, then grind to a coarse powder.
Heat oil, saute onion until golden, add garlic, ginger and the roasted spice powder.
Add the chicken and water, and simmer 18-20 minutes until tender.
Serve hot with bhakri or rice.
why_it_works: Vidarbha's dry-roasted whole-spice technique, including sesame, gives a genuinely different flavour base from the coconut-heavy Kolhapuri or Malvani curries in this batch
Third distinct Maharashtrian regional chicken curry style represented, alongside Kolhapur and Konkan
Nagpur-Vidarbha cuisine known for its bold, complex spicing

name: ZITLAS Sprouted Matki Amti Bowl
description: Sprouted matki cooked in a tangy, kokum-soured amti gravy — a distinct preparation from the plain Matki Usal already in the database by its sourness and gravy consistency.
instructions: Heat oil, saute onion until golden, add goda masala.
Add boiled matki, kokum and a little jaggery, along with water to form a gravy; simmer 10-12 minutes.
Serve hot with rice or bhakri.
why_it_works: Kokum's souring gives this a genuinely different, tangier profile from the plain, less-sour Matki Usal Bowl already in the database
Amti's sweet-sour-spicy balance is a distinctly Maharashtrian approach to legume cookery
Same base legume, different, more complex preparation

name: ZITLAS Paneer Bharli Vangi-Style Stuffed Capsicum
description: The peanut-coconut stuffing technique from Bharli Vangi adapted into capsicum with paneer added for extra protein — a distinct vessel and protein combination from the original eggplant version.
instructions: Mix ground peanuts, grated coconut, crumbled paneer and goda masala into a thick stuffing.
Fill the capsicum halves with the mixture.
Heat oil in a kadai, place the stuffed capsicum in, add a little water, cover and simmer 15-18 minutes until the capsicum softens.
Serve hot.
why_it_works: Adapts the distinctive Bharli Vangi peanut-coconut stuffing technique to a different vessel and adds paneer, giving a genuinely higher-protein variant of the original eggplant dish
Two protein sources combined directly in the stuffing
Capsicum cooks faster than whole eggplant, making this a quicker dinner option

name: ZITLAS Solkadhi and Rice Light Dinner Bowl
description: A small portion of rice paired with solkadhi as a light, easily digestible dinner — distinct from the breakfast Solkadhi and Roasted Chana Combo by being a warm-rice pairing rather than a cold drink-and-snack combo.
instructions: Soak kokum in a little warm water.
Whisk the kokum water into coconut milk with garlic and cumin.
Pour the solkadhi over warm rice in a bowl, like a thin, tangy soup-rice combination.
Eat immediately while the rice is still warm.
why_it_works: Rice-and-solkadhi pairing is a traditional light-dinner combination, distinct from the drink-and-snack breakfast pairing already in the database
Very light and easy to digest before sleep
Minimal cooking required

name: ZITLAS Steamed Rice Dumplings with Soya Keema Filling
description: A modak-shaped steamed dumpling filled with spiced soya keema instead of the moong filling used in the breakfast version — a distinct protein filling for the same traditional shape.
ingredients: Soya chunks, rehydrated and finely chopped — 70 g
instructions: Knead rice flour with boiling water into a smooth dough.
Cook the finely chopped soya chunks with ginger-garlic paste and garam masala until well spiced and slightly dry.
Shape small discs of dough, pleat the edges, fill with the soya keema, and gather into the traditional modak shape.
Steam in a pressure cooker (without the whistle) for 12-15 minutes.
Serve warm.
why_it_works: Soya keema filling gives notably more protein than the moong-filled breakfast version, better suited to a muscle-gain-focused dinner
Same distinctive pleated shape and steaming technique, different protein purpose
Higher protein density for an evening meal

name: ZITLAS Bhakri Pizza-Style Zunka Topped
description: A jowar bhakri spread with zunka and topped with vegetables, briefly grilled — a playful, family-friendly presentation distinct from serving zunka and bhakri as two separate components.
instructions: Cook two bhakris on a tawa as usual.
Prepare zunka as normal with besan, turmeric and mustard seeds.
Spread the zunka thickly over each bhakri and scatter chopped vegetables on top.
Return to the tawa briefly, covered, to warm through and soften the vegetables slightly.
Slice like a pizza and serve.
why_it_works: Combining zunka and bhakri into a single topped, sliced format is a genuinely different presentation from serving them as two separate components
Family-friendly, fun way to get kids interested in a traditional dish
Same core ingredients, different construction

name: ZITLAS Family-Style Masale Bhaat Platter
description: A larger-batch version of Masale Bhaat with added paneer and a wider vegetable mix, plated as a shared family platter — distinct from the individual lunch portion already in this batch.
instructions: Heat oil, temper whole spices, add mixed vegetables and saute 4-5 minutes.
Add rice, goda masala and paneer cubes, mixing gently.
Add water in the standard ratio and pressure cook for 2-3 whistles.
Fluff gently (to avoid breaking the paneer) and serve family-style on a large platter.
why_it_works: Paneer addition and larger batch size make this a genuinely different meal-planning purpose from the individual lunch Masale Bhaat in this batch — a shared family dinner rather than a solo lunch
Higher protein than the lunch version thanks to the paneer
Same base technique, different scale and composition

name: ZITLAS Post-Workout Soya Amti Bowl
description: Soya chunks cooked in a tangy kokum-soured amti gravy over rice, specifically timed and portioned for right after an evening workout — a protein-and-carb dinner with a deliberate post-exercise purpose.
instructions: Heat oil, temper with goda masala.
Add soya chunks, kokum and a little jaggery with water to form a gravy; simmer 10-12 minutes.
Serve hot over rice within 45-60 minutes of finishing an evening workout.
why_it_works: Explicitly timed for the post-workout window, with a protein-and-carb balance suited to evening training recovery, unlike the general-purpose amti bowls already in this batch
High protein from soya combined with easily digestible rice carbohydrates
Kokum's tang keeps this from feeling heavy despite being eaten after exercise

name: ZITLAS Mixed Sprouts Amti Dinner Bowl
description: A kokum-soured amti made from a mix of sprouted legumes rather than a single pulse — a broader-legume-base dinner distinct from the single-legume amti and usal preparations already in this batch.
instructions: Heat oil, saute onion until golden, add goda masala.
Add the mixed sprouts, kokum and a little jaggery with water to form a gravy; simmer 10-12 minutes.
Serve hot with bhakri or rice.
why_it_works: Combining several sprouted legumes gives a broader amino acid profile than any single-pulse amti or usal already in this batch
Kokum souring ties it to the same Maharashtrian amti family as the Sprouted Matki Amti Bowl
Genuinely different legume composition, same reliable regional technique
